claims.source: An important insight into the evolutionary history of NPY-related peptides was obtained with identification of a PP-like immunoreactive peptide in a protostome invertebrate, the platyhelminth Moniezia expansa (Maule et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original discovery paper.

claims.claim: The invertebrate NPY homolog from Moniezia expansa is a 39-residue peptide with the C-terminal tyrosine (Y) substituted with a phenylalanine (F) and was named neuropeptide F (NPF).
claims.source: Sequencing revealed a 39-residue peptide with a similar structure to NPY, but with the C-terminal tyrosine (Y) substituted with a phenylalanine (F). Hence, this invertebrate NPY homolog was named neuropeptide F (NPF) (Maule et al., 1991).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original sequencing study.

claims.claim: NPF-type neuropeptides have been identified in protostome invertebrates including platyhelminths, molluscs, annelids and arthropods.
claims.source: Subsequently, NPF-type neuropeptides have been identified in other protostome invertebrates, including other platyhelminths (Curry et al., 1992), molluscs (Leung et al., 1992; Rajpara et al., 1992), annelids (Veenstra, 2011; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Bauknecht and Jékely, 2015) and arthropods (Brown et al., 1999), and these peptides typically have a conserved C-terminal RPRFamide motif and range in length from 36 to 40 residues (Fadda et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to discovery papers in different taxa.

claims.claim: NPF-type peptides typically have a conserved C-terminal RPRFamide motif and range in length from 36 to 40 residues.
claims.source: Subsequently, NPF-type neuropeptides have been identified in other protostome invertebrates, including other platyhelminths (Curry et al., 1992), molluscs (Leung et al., 1992; Rajpara et al., 1992), annelids (Veenstra, 2011; Conzelmann et al., 2013; Bauknecht and Jékely, 2015) and arthropods (Brown et al., 1999), and these peptides typically have a conserved C-terminal RPRFamide motif and range in length from 36 to 40 residues (Fadda et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review summarizing structural features of NPF peptides.

claims.claim: Two novel neuropeptides, ARGPQLRLRFamide and APSLRLRFamide, were discovered in the Colorado potato beetle Leptinotarsa decemlineata using antibodies to M. expansa NPF.
claims.source: Interestingly, this resulted in the discovery of two novel neuropeptides, ARGPQLRLRFamide and APSLRLRFamide, in the Colorado potato beetle Leptinotarsa decemlineata (Spittaels et al., 1996).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original discovery paper.

claims.claim: The peptides ARGPQLRLRFamide and APSLRLRFamide were renamed as short neuropeptide F (sNPF) because they are much shorter in length than NPF.
claims.source: As these peptides were isolated using antibodies to M. expansa NPF, they were originally referred to as NPF-related peptides. However, because they are much shorter in length than NPF, they were later renamed as short neuropeptide F (sNPF) (Vanden Broeck, 2001) and homologs were identified in other insects (Schoofs et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the naming and subsequent identification papers.

claims.claim: sNPF-type peptides and precursors exhibit too many differences to be considered orthologs of NPY/NPF-type peptides and precursors.
claims.source: Furthermore, alignment of NPY-type peptides and precursors from vertebrates with NPF-type and sNPF-type peptides and precursors from protostomes revealed that whilst NPF-type peptides are clearly orthologs of vertebrate NPY-type peptides, sNPF-type peptides and precursors exhibit too many differences to be considered orthologs of NPY/NPF-type peptides and precursors (Nässel and Wegener, 2011).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a comparative analysis study.

claims.claim: Chordate NPY-type and invertebrate NPF-type neuropeptides are orthologous based on similarity-based clustering methods.
claims.source: Further evidence that chordate NPY-type and invertebrate NPF-type neuropeptides are orthologous has been provided by similarity-based clustering methods, showing that the NPY-type and NPF-type precursors form a pan-bilaterian cluster, whereas sNPF-type precursors form a separate cluster (Jékely, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a clustering analysis study.

claims.claim: A receptor for sNPF-type peptides was first identified in Drosophila melanogaster with the deorphanisation of the GPCR CG7395.
claims.source: A receptor for sNPF-type peptides was first identified in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster with the deorphanisation of the GPCR CG7395 (Mertens et al., 2002), which was previously annotated as a homolog of mammalian NPY-type receptors.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the original deorphanisation study.

claims.claim: sNPF receptors have been identified in other insects following the initial discovery in Drosophila melanogaster.
claims.source: Subsequently, sNPF receptors have been identified in other insects (Chen and Pietrantonio, 2006; Garczynski et al., 2007; Yamanaka et al., 2008; Dillen et al., 2013; Dillen et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2017; Ma et al., 2017; Christ et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to receptor identification studies in various insect species.

claims.claim: In Drosophila melanogaster, overexpression of sNPF increases food intake in both larvae and adults, whilst loss-of-function sNPF-mutants exhibited reduced food intake.
claims.source: For example, in D. melanogaster overexpression of sNPF increases food intake both in larvae and adults, whilst loss-of-function sNPF-mutants exhibited reduced food intake (Lee et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a functional study in Drosophila.

claims.claim: An expanded family of neuropeptide receptors in C. elegans that had originally been annotated as NPY/NPF-type receptors were found to be orthologs of insect sNPF-receptors.
claims.source: Thus, an expanded family of neuropeptide receptors in the nematode C. elegans that had originally been annotated as NPY/NPF-type receptors (Cardoso et al., 2012) were found to be orthologs of insect sNPF-receptors (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original annotation and the phylogenetic reclassification studies.

claims.claim: sNPF-type peptides and a cognate receptor have been characterised in the bivalve mollusc Crassostrea gigas.
claims.source: Subsequently, sNPF-type peptides and a cognate receptor have been characterised in the bivalve mollusc Crassostrea gigas, confirming the occurrence of this signalling system in the lophotrochozoan branch of the protostomes (Bigot et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a characterization study in oysters.

claims.claim: NPY/NPF receptor-related proteins occur in the echinoderm Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
claims.source: Phylogenetic analysis of bilaterian G-protein coupled neuropeptide receptors has demonstrated the occurrence of NPY/NPF receptor-related proteins in ambulacrarians – the echinoderm Strongylocentrotus purpuratus and the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a phylogenetic analysis study.

claims.claim: The precursor of a putative NPY/NPF-type peptide was identified in Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
claims.source: Furthermore, the precursor of a putative NPY/NPF-type peptide was identified in S. kowalevskii (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies identifying the precursor.

claims.claim: A candidate NPY/NPF-type precursor has been identified in the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae.
claims.source: A candidate NPY/NPF-type precursor has also been identified in the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae, but an NPY/NPF-type receptor has yet to be identified in this species (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies identifying the precursor.

claims.claim: A family of neuropeptide precursor-type proteins in echinoderms contain a peptide that shares sequence similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides.
claims.source: A more recent finding was the discovery of a family neuropeptide precursor-type proteins in echinoderms that contain a peptide that shares sequence similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides (Zandawala et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a discovery study.

claims.claim: The sequence of a transcript encoding the precursor of an NPY-like neuropeptide has been reported previously based on analysis of neural transcriptome sequence data from the starfish A. rubens.
claims.source: The sequence of a transcript (contig 1060225; GenBank accession number MK033631.1) encoding the precursor of an NPY-like neuropeptide has been reported previously based on analysis of neural transcriptome sequence data from the starfish A. rubens (Zandawala et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous transcriptome study and a GenBank accession number.

claims.claim: A cDNA encoding the A. rubens NPY-like neuropeptide precursor was cloned and sequenced, revealing an open reading frame encoding a 108-residue protein comprising a predicted 19-residue signal peptide, a 23-residue NPY-like peptide sequence with an N-terminal glutamine residue and a C-terminal glycine residue, followed by a putative monobasic cleavage site.
claims.source: Here, a cDNA encoding this precursor was cloned and sequenced, revealing that the open reading frame encodes a 108-residue protein comprising a predicted 19-residue signal peptide, a 23-residue NPY-like peptide sequence with an N-terminal glutamine residue and a C-terminal glycine residue, followed by a putative monobasic cleavage site (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental cloning and sequencing data, with results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Analysis of radial nerve cord extracts using mass spectrometry revealed the presence of a peptide with the structure pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2.
claims.source: Analysis of radial nerve cord extracts using mass spectrometry (LC-MS-MS) revealed the presence of a peptide with the structure pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2, showing that the N-terminal glutamine and C-terminal glycine in the precursor peptide are post-translationally converted to a pyroglutamate residue and an amide group, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The N-terminal glutamine and C-terminal glycine in the precursor peptide are post-translationally converted to a pyroglutamate residue and an amide group, respectively.
claims.source: Analysis of radial nerve cord extracts using mass spectrometry (LC-MS-MS) revealed the presence of a peptide with the structure pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2, showing that the N-terminal glutamine and C-terminal glycine in the precursor peptide are post-translationally converted to a pyroglutamate residue and an amide group, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on mass spectrometry data showing post-translational modifications.

claims.claim: The A. rubens neuropeptide and orthologs from other echinoderms share sequence similarity with both PrRP-type neuropeptides and NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides.
claims.source: Alignment of the sequences of the A. rubens neuropeptide and orthologs from other echinoderms with related peptides in other taxa revealed that they share sequence similarity with both PrRP-type neuropeptides (Figure 1A) and with NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figures 1A and 1B.

claims.claim: The echinoderm peptides comprise 22–25 residues and are similar in length to vertebrate PrRPs, which are 20–31 residues as full-length peptides.
claims.source: However, the echinoderm peptides comprise 22–25 residues and are similar in length to vertebrate PrRPs, which are 20–31 residues as full-length peptides and in some species can occur as N-terminally truncated peptides due the presence of a monobasic cleavage site (Hinuma et al., 1998; Tachibana and Sakamoto, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence length comparisons and is supported by citations to studies on PrRP structure.

claims.claim: NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides are longer peptides ranging in length from 36 to 40 residues.
claims.source: This contrasts with NPY/NPF-type neuropeptides, which are longer peptides ranging in length from 36 to 40 residues (Fadda et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review on NPY/NPF peptide structure.

claims.claim: Novel neuropeptides that share sequence similarity with the echinoderm neuropeptides and with vertebrate PrRPs were identified in the hemichordate S. kowalevskii and the cephalochordate B. floridae.
claims.source: Furthermore, by analysing sequence data from the hemichordate S. kowalevskii and the cephalochordate B. floridae, here we identified novel neuropeptides that share sequence similarity with the echinoderm neuropeptides and with vertebrate PrRPs (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis and alignment shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: The echinoderm peptides lack two proline (P) residues that are a conserved feature of the N-terminal region of many NPY/NPF-type peptides.
claims.source: Contrastingly, the echinoderm peptides lack two proline (P) residues that are a conserved feature of the N-terminal region of many NPY/NPF-type peptides, with the exception of some peptides that have only one of these proline residues and a peptide in the cephalochordate Branchiostoma floridae that has neither (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Four residues (tyrosine, leucine, tyrosine, and isoleucine) are highly conserved in bilaterian NPY/NPF-type peptides and have been shown to be important for the formation of the three-dimensional structure in vertebrate NPY-type peptides.
claims.source: Furthermore, there are four other residues that are highly conserved in bilaterian NPY/NPF-type peptides - tyrosine (Y), leucine (L), tyrosine (Y), and isoleucine (I) residues, which are marked with arrowheads in Figure 1B. These residues have been shown to be important for the formation of the three-dimensional structure in vertebrate NPY-type peptides (Blundell et al., 1981; Glover et al., 1983; Glover et al., 1984; Allen et al., 1987), so these residues may likewise be important for NPF receptor activation and bioactivity.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence conservation analysis and is supported by citations to structural studies.

claims.claim: None of the four conserved residues important for NPY/NPF structure are present in the echinoderm peptides.
claims.source: Importantly, none of these residues are present in the echinoderm peptides.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: All but one of the six conserved residues in NPY/NPF-type peptides are present in a peptide from the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii.
claims.source: It is noteworthy, however, that all but one of the aforementioned six conserved residues in NPY/NPF-type peptides are present in a peptide from a species belonging to a sister phylum of the echinoderms – the hemichordate Saccoglossus kowalevskii (Figure 1B; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1B and is supported by citations.

claims.claim: A common characteristic of echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes and chordate PrRP genes is the presence of an intron that interrupts the coding sequence at a position corresponding to the N-terminal or central region of the peptides.
claims.source: This revealed that a common characteristic is the presence of an intron that interrupts the coding sequence at a position corresponding to the N-terminal or central region of the echinoderm PrRP-like peptides and vertebrate PrRPs.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene structure analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: In echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes and vertebrate PrRP genes, the intron interrupts the coding sequence in the same frame, at a position between the first and second nucleotide of the interrupted codon (a phase one intron).
claims.source: Furthermore, in echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes and vertebrate PrRP genes the intron interrupts the coding sequence in the same frame, at a position between the first and second nucleotide of the interrupted codon (a phase one intron), which is denoted by +1 in Figure 2.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene structure analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Genes encoding novel precursors of PrRP-like peptides in S. kowalevskii and B. floridae also have a phase one intron.
claims.source: Genes encoding novel precursors of PrRP-like peptides in S. kowalevskii and B. floridae also have a phase one intron.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene structure analysis shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The presence of a conserved intron in the same frame in echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes, the two S. kowalevskii PrRP-like peptide genes and chordate PrRP-type genes supports the hypothesis that the echinoderm and hemichordate PrRP-like peptides are orthologs of chordate PrRP-type neuropeptides.
claims.source: The presence of a conserved intron in the same frame in echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes, the two S. kowalevskii PrRP-like peptide genes and chordate PrRP-type genes supports our hypothesis that the echinoderm and hemichordate PrRP-like peptides are orthologs of chordate PrRP-type neuropeptides.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from gene structure conservation analysis.

claims.claim: A conserved feature of NPY/NPF genes is an intron that interrupts the coding sequence for NPY/NPF-type peptides, with the intron located between the second and third nucleotide of the codon for the arginine residue of the C-terminal RF or RY dipeptide.
claims.source: Previous studies have reported that a conserved feature of NPY/NPF genes is an intron that interrupts the coding sequence for NPY/NPF-type peptides, with the intron located between the second and third nucleotide of the codon for the arginine residue of the C-terminal RF or RY dipeptide (Mair et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a previous gene structure study.

claims.claim: In echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes, the intron does not interrupt the codon for the arginine of the C-terminal RF or RY motif, but instead is located between the first and second nucleotide of the codon for a residue located in the N-terminal or central regions of echinoderm PrRP-like peptides.
claims.source: Thus, it does not interrupt the codon for the arginine of the C-terminal RF or RY motif, but instead it is located between the first and second nucleotide of the codon for a residue located in the N-terminal or central regions of echinoderm PrRP-like peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene structure comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Typically in NPY/NPF genes there is another intron that interrupts the coding sequence in the C-terminal region of the precursor protein, whereas in the echinoderm PrRP-like peptide precursor genes the coding sequence for the C-terminal region of the precursor protein is not interrupted by an intron.
claims.source: Another difference is that typically in NPY/NPF genes there is another intron that interrupts the coding sequence in the C-terminal region of the precursor protein, whereas in the echinoderm PrRP-like peptide precursor genes the coding sequence for the C-terminal region of the precursor protein is not interrupted by an intron (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene structure comparison shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: A transcript (contig 1120879) encoding a 386-residue protein was identified as the best hit when using NPY-type, NPF-type, PrRP-type and sNPF-type receptors as queries for similarity-based analysis of A. rubens neural transcriptome sequence data.
claims.source: Using receptor sequences of H. sapiens NPY-type, D. melanogaster NPF-type, H. sapiens PrRP-type and D. melanogaster sNPF-type receptors as queries for similarity-based analysis of A. rubens neural transcriptome sequence data, a transcript (contig 1120879) encoding a 386-residue protein was identified as the best hit (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on BLAST analysis of transcriptome data.

claims.claim: Homologs of the A. rubens protein encoded by contig 1120879 were identified in other echinoderms including the starfish A. planci, the sea urchin S. purpuratus and the sea cucumber A. japonicus.
claims.source: Furthermore, homologs of the A. rubens protein encoded by contig 1120879 were also identified in other echinoderms for which genome sequences have been obtained, including the starfish A. planci, the sea urchin S. purpuratus and the sea cucumber A. japonicus, and importantly no other NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors were identified in these species.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on BLAST analysis of genome data from multiple echinoderm species.

claims.claim: No other NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors were identified in the echinoderms A. planci, S. purpuratus and A. japonicus.
claims.source: Furthermore, homologs of the A. rubens protein encoded by contig 1120879 were also identified in other echinoderms for which genome sequences have been obtained, including the starfish A. planci, the sea urchin S. purpuratus and the sea cucumber A. japonicus, and importantly no other NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors were identified in these species.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comprehensive BLAST analysis of genome data.

claims.claim: Cluster-based analysis using CLANS revealed three main clusters: a cluster comprising the outgroup receptors (tachykinin/luqin), a cluster comprising NPY/NPF-type receptors, and a cluster comprising sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors.
claims.source: This analysis revealed three main clusters: 1. a cluster comprising the outgroup receptors (tachykinin/luqin), 2. a cluster comprising NPY/NPF-type receptors and 3. a cluster comprising sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on CLANS clustering analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The echinoderm receptors showed stronger connections with the sNPF/PrRP receptor cluster than with the NPY/NPF receptor cluster in CLANS analysis.
claims.source: Interestingly, the echinoderm receptors showed stronger connections with the sNPF/PrRP receptor cluster (Figure 3, black square) than with the NPY/NPF receptor cluster.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on CLANS clustering analysis shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors are orthologous based on cluster-based analysis of receptor sequences.
claims.source: These findings indicate that sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors are orthologous, as has been proposed previously based on cluster-based analysis of receptor sequences (Jékely, 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on CLANS analysis and is supported by a citation to a previous clustering study.

claims.claim: NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors in echinoderms are not orthologs of NPY/NPF-type receptors but are orthologs of sNPF/PrRP-type receptors.
claims.source: Furthermore, these findings indicate that NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptors in echinoderms are not orthologs of NPY/NPF-type receptors but are orthologs of sNPF/PrRP-type receptors.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on inference from CLANS clustering analysis.

claims.claim: The lines linking the echinoderm receptors and nematode sNPF-type receptors with other sNPF/PrRP-type receptors in CLANS are quite long, which is indicative of sequence divergence.
claims.source: However, it is noteworthy that the lines linking the echinoderm receptors and nematode sNPF-type receptors with other sNPF/PrRP-type receptors in CLANS are quite long (Figure 3), which is indicative of sequence divergence.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on interpretation of CLANS clustering results shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: In phylogenetic analysis using the maximum likelihood method, the echinoderm receptors are positioned within a branch comprising NPY/NPF-type, PrRP-type and sNPF-type receptors.
claims.source: This revealed that the echinoderm receptors are positioned within a branch of the phylogenetic tree that comprises NPY/NPF-type, PrRP-type and sNPF-type receptors, with the other receptor types included in the analysis occupying an outgroup position (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The echinoderm receptors are positioned in a clade comprising sNPF-type receptors, with bootstrap support of >90%.
claims.source: More specifically, the echinoderm receptors are positioned in a clade comprising sNPF-type receptors, with bootstrap support of >90%, indicating that the echinoderm receptors are orthologs of protostome sNPF-type receptors.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis with bootstrap support shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors do not form a monophyletic clade in the phylogenetic tree.
claims.source: However, it is noteworthy that sNPF-type receptors and PrRP-type receptors do not form a monophyletic clade as would be expected for orthologous receptors.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on observation of the phylogenetic tree structure in Figure 4.

claims.claim: The lack of monophyly between sNPF-type and PrRP-type receptors may be a consequence of sequence divergence in the echinoderm and nematode sNPF/PrRP-type receptors.
claims.source: This may be a consequence of sequence divergence in the echinoderm and nematode sNPF/PrRP-type receptors that is reflected in the long branches leading to these receptors.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the phylogenetic tree topology.

claims.claim: There is a long branch leading to the echinoderm receptor clade in the phylogenetic tree.
claims.source: Accordingly, it is noteworthy that in the phylogenetic tree (Figure 4) there is a long branch leading to the echinoderm receptor clade and likewise nematode sNPF-type receptors also have long branches (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on observation of branch lengths in the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Sequence identity between echinoderm PrRP-type peptides and protostome sNPF-type peptides is restricted to a few residues in the C-terminal regions of the peptides.
claims.source: This revealed that sequence identity is restricted to a few residues in the C-terminal regions of the peptides and, furthermore, the echinoderm PrRP-type peptides are much longer than protostome sNPF-type peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The echinoderm PrRP-type peptides are much longer than protostome sNPF-type peptides.
claims.source: This revealed that sequence identity is restricted to a few residues in the C-terminal regions of the peptides and, furthermore, the echinoderm PrRP-type peptides are much longer than protostome sNPF-type peptides (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on sequence length comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Protostome sNPF-type neuropeptide precursors typically give rise to multiple sNPF-type peptides, whereas echinoderm PrRP-type precursors contain a single PrRP-type neuropeptide that is located adjacent to the signal peptide.
claims.source: Another difference is that protostome sNPF-type neuropeptide precursors typically give rise to multiple sNPF-type peptides, whereas echinoderm PrRP-type precursors are similar to chordate PrRP-type precursors in containing a single PrRP-type neuropeptide that is located adjacent to the signal peptide (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on comparison of precursor structures shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Comparison of the exon/intron structure of the genes encoding PrRP-type precursors in echinoderms and sNPF-type precursors in protostomes revealed limited similarity.
claims.source: Accordingly, comparison of the exon/intron structure of the genes encoding PrRP-type precursors in echinoderms and sNPF-type precursors in protostomes also revealed limited similarity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on gene structure comparison shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Analysis of the sequence of Ar-sNPF/PrRPR using Protter revealed seven predicted transmembrane domains.
claims.source: Analysis of the sequence of Ar-sNPF/PrRPR using Protter revealed seven predicted transmembrane domains, as expected for a GPCR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on computational prediction of protein structure shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: ArPrRP at a concentration of 10−5 M triggers luminescence responses in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells that were approximately five times the background luminescence.
claims.source: This revealed that ArPrRP at a concentration of 10−5 M triggers luminescence responses (defined as 100%) in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells that were approximately five times the background luminescence detected with the assay media used to dissolve the peptide (Figure 5A), demonstrating that ArPrRP acts as a ligand for the receptor.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental receptor assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: ArPrRP acts as a ligand for the Ar-sNPF/PrRPR receptor.
claims.source: This revealed that ArPrRP at a concentration of 10−5 M triggers luminescence responses (defined as 100%) in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells that were approximately five times the background luminescence detected with the assay media used to dissolve the peptide (Figure 5A), demonstrating that ArPrRP acts as a ligand for the receptor.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental receptor assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: ArPrRP induced dose-dependent luminescence in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells with a half-maximal response concentration (EC50) of 1.5 × 10−10 M.
claims.source: Furthermore, ArPrRP induced dose-dependent luminescence in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells with a half-maximal response concentration (EC50) of 1.5 × 10−10 M (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on dose-response experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: No response to ArPrRP was observed in CHO-K1 cells transfected with the vector alone.
claims.source: Importantly, no response to ArPrRP was observed in CHO-K1 cells transfected with the vector alone, demonstrating that the signal observed in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells exposed to ArPrRP can be attributed to activation of the transfected receptor (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on negative control experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The C-terminal pentapeptide of ArPrRP (LNPRFamide) did not induce luminescence responses in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells.
claims.source: However, this peptide did not induce luminescence responses in CHO-Ar-sNPF/PrRPR cells (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This claim is based on experimental receptor assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The 22-residue amidated peptide ArPrRP is the natural ligand for Ar-sNPF/PrRPR in A. rubens.
claims.source: Therefore, we conclude that the 22-residue amidated peptide ArPrRP is the natural ligand for Ar-sNPF/PrRPR in A. rubens.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on experimental data showing that the full-length peptide activates the receptor while the truncated peptide does not.

results.result: The authors cloned and sequenced a cDNA encoding an A. rubens neuropeptide precursor and confirmed the mature peptide structure (pQDRSKAMQAERTGQLRRLNPRF-NH2) using mass spectrometry, demonstrating post-translational modifications including N-terminal pyroglutamation and C-terminal amidation.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37 provide converging evidence from molecular cloning (C35) and mass spectrometry (C36-C37) that establish both the precursor structure and the mature peptide form. The mass spectrometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B directly confirms the post-translational modifications predicted from the precursor sequence.

results.result: Sequence alignment analysis reveals that echinoderm peptides share greater similarity with PrRP-type peptides (22-25 residues) than with NPY/NPF-type peptides (36-40 residues), lacking key conserved residues characteristic of NPY/NPF peptides but sharing features with chordate PrRPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C45 collectively demonstrate through sequence alignments (Figures 1A and 1B) that echinoderm peptides are more similar to PrRP than NPY/NPF based on length, conserved residues, and structural features. The absence of four key NPY/NPF-conserved residues (C43-C44) and the presence of PrRP-like features provide strong evidence for orthology with PrRP rather than NPY/NPF.

results.result: Gene structure analysis shows that echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes share a conserved phase-one intron position with chordate PrRP genes, supporting orthology between these peptide families.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 demonstrate through gene structure analysis (Figure 2) that the conserved intron position and phase in echinoderm, hemichordate, and chordate PrRP genes provides independent evidence for orthology. This genomic synteny evidence complements the sequence similarity data and strengthens the orthology hypothesis.

results.result: The intron structure of echinoderm PrRP-like peptide genes differs fundamentally from NPY/NPF genes, with the intron positioned in the N-terminal/central region rather than interrupting the C-terminal arginine codon.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C52 establish clear structural differences between echinoderm PrRP-like genes and NPY/NPF genes through comparative gene structure analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). The different intron positions and phases provide strong negative evidence against NPY/NPF orthology.

results.result: BLAST analysis of echinoderm transcriptome and genome data identified a single NPY/NPF/PrRP/sNPF-type receptor in multiple echinoderm species, with no other receptors of this type present.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C55 describe systematic BLAST searches across multiple echinoderm species that consistently identified only one candidate receptor. The comprehensive nature of the search and consistency across species supports the conclusion, though the absence of evidence is not definitive proof of absence.

results.result: CLANS cluster-based analysis reveals that echinoderm receptors cluster more strongly with sNPF/PrRP-type receptors than with NPY/NPF-type receptors, indicating orthology with the sNPF/PrRP receptor family despite evidence of sequence divergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C60 present CLANS clustering results (Figure 3) showing three distinct receptor clusters with echinoderm receptors positioned within the sNPF/PrRP cluster. The long connection lines (C60) appropriately acknowledge sequence divergence, which is consistent with the phylogenetic findings. The clustering methodology is well-established for receptor classification.

results.result: Maximum likelihood phylogenetic analysis positions echinoderm receptors within a clade of sNPF-type receptors with >90% bootstrap support, though sNPF and PrRP receptors do not form a monophyletic clade, possibly due to sequence divergence.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C65 present phylogenetic analysis (Figure 4) with strong bootstrap support (>90%) for the placement of echinoderm receptors with sNPF receptors. The lack of monophyly between sNPF and PrRP receptors (C63) is acknowledged and explained by sequence divergence (C64-C65), which is a reasonable interpretation given the long branch lengths observed.

results.result: Comparison of echinoderm PrRP-type and protostome sNPF-type peptides reveals limited sequence similarity restricted to C-terminal regions, with echinoderm peptides being longer and having different precursor and gene structures.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69 document substantial differences between echinoderm PrRP-type and protostome sNPF-type peptides through sequence, precursor, and gene structure comparisons (Figure 4—figure supplements 1-2). These differences are important for understanding the evolutionary divergence between these orthologous systems.

results.result: Functional receptor assays demonstrate that ArPrRP is a potent and selective ligand for Ar-sNPF/PrRPR with an EC50 of 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ M, while truncated peptides and unrelated neuropeptides do not activate the receptor.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 provide comprehensive experimental validation through dose-response assays (Figure 5), negative controls (C74), and specificity tests (C75, C77). The EC50 value is in the nanomolar range typical of neuropeptide receptors, and the controls appropriately demonstrate specificity. This is the key experimental result linking the peptide to its receptor.

results.result: NPY/NPF-type signaling has been lost in echinoderms based on the absence of NPY/NPF-type peptides and receptors in comprehensive transcriptome and genome analyses.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C78, and C55 collectively establish the loss of NPY/NPF signaling through negative evidence from multiple echinoderm species. While absence of evidence requires caution, the comprehensive nature of the genomic searches and consistency across multiple species provides strong support for this conclusion.

results.result: PrRP-type and sNPF-type signaling systems are orthologous and originated as a paralog of NPY/NPF-type signaling in Urbilateria, with echinoderms providing the missing evolutionary link between vertebrate PrRP and protostome sNPF systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C58, C88, and C99 represent the main evolutionary conclusion of the study, supported by sequence analysis, gene structure, phylogenetic analysis, and functional validation. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence (peptide sequences, gene structures, receptor phylogeny, and ligand-receptor pairing) provides strong support for this evolutionary hypothesis.

results.result: The C. elegans FLP-27 precursor is likely an ortholog of NPY/NPF-type peptides based on gene structure analysis showing a characteristic intron position, and the derived peptide likely acts as a ligand for NPR-11 and/or NPR-12 receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C85 propose a hypothesis about C. elegans NPY/NPF signaling based on gene structure (C84) and phylogenetic positioning of receptors. However, this remains speculative (C85 uses "likely") without experimental validation of the ligand-receptor interaction. The gene structure evidence (C84) is solid, but functional validation is needed.

results.result: The authors propose that PrRP-type peptides in deuterostomes more closely resemble the ancestral PrRP/sNPF signaling system in Urbilateria, with protostome sNPF-type peptides representing greater divergence from the ancestral condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C98 present speculative evolutionary scenarios about ancestral characteristics. While based on comparative analysis of peptide and precursor structures, these are explicitly acknowledged as speculation (C92, C94-C96). The hypothesis is reasonable but lacks direct evidence about ancestral states and represents inference rather than demonstrated fact.

results.result: The peptide MDANAFRMSFamide activates C. elegans receptor NPR-11 but shares little sequence similarity with NPY/NPF-type peptides and requires unusually high concentrations (10-30 µM) for activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C82 accurately report findings from cited literature (Chalasani et al., 2010) regarding NPR-11 activation. The high EC50 values (C82) appropriately raise questions about whether this is the natural ligand, supporting the authors' subsequent proposal about FLP-27 as an alternative candidate.

results.result: The introduction establishes the evolutionary context of neuropeptide signaling systems, documenting the prior identification of NPY/NPF, PrRP, and sNPF peptides and receptors across bilaterian phyla.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C34 provide background information supported by extensive citations to prior literature. These claims establish the scientific context for the current study and are appropriately referenced. As background material, these claims are well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Computational analysis using Protter predicts seven transmembrane domains in the Ar-sNPF/PrRPR sequence, consistent with GPCR structure.
results.evaluation: Claim C70 reports a standard computational prediction of transmembrane domains (Figure 5—figure supplement 1). Seven transmembrane domains is the expected structure for GPCRs, and this prediction is consistent with the receptor's classification. This is a routine structural prediction that supports the receptor's identity.

results.result: Loss of NPY/NPF-type signaling has been reported in urochordates.
results.evaluation: Claim C79 accurately cites prior work (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013) documenting NPY/NPF loss in urochordates. This provides comparative context for the echinoderm finding but is not a novel result of this study.
